lesson_title: The Pool Is Deeper Than It Looks
hook_text: Stand a pencil in a glass of water and it snaps in half. Look into a pool and the bottom rises towards you. Both are lies told by light.
clip_script: Stand a pencil in a glass of water. It looks snapped. Pull it out: perfectly straight. Light travels fast in air and slows down in water and glass. Cross the boundary at a slant and that change of speed bends the light. Slowing down, it bends towards the normal; speeding up, it bends away. Your brain assumes light always travels in straight lines, so it places things in the wrong spot. That is why a swimming pool looks only about three quarters as deep as it really is, and why you should always check real depth before you jump. On a hot Karoo road, layers of hot air bend light from the sky into your eyes, and you see shimmering puddles that are not there. Curve the glass on purpose and you get a lens: fat in the middle to bring light together and magnify, thin in the middle to spread it out.
visual_style: A whiteboard glass with a snapped-looking pencil, then rays bending at the water surface traced back by dashed lines to a raised image, then a hot road with curving rays and a mirage, then convex and concave lenses.
pacing: A quick trick, a clear rule, then real-world examples.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and draw a refraction ray diagram.
